state.misconception_label: Confuses rest and movement on a distance time graph

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: This graph shows how far Fido the dog is from his home. What might the negative-sloping section represent? ![A graph with time (secs) on the horizontal axis and distance (m) on the vertical axis. The graph starts at the origin, travels in a straight line up and right, travels horizontally, then travels in a straight line down and right back to the x-axis. ](). I got Fido has fallen asleep because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you're watching a movie where the main character goes on a journey. When the character is moving away from home, the distance from home increases. But when the character starts heading back, the distance decreases. So, in the graph, the negative-sloping section might represent Fido returning home, not falling asleep. Let's walk through why that is the case.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh right, so when the line goes down, that means the distance is getting smaller, so Fido must be getting closer to home? But I'm still a bit confused - I thought a negative slope meant something bad was happening, like he was stuck or something. Why does going down on the graph mean he's moving back towards home?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you're playing a game where you have to walk back to the starting point. As you walk towards the starting point, the distance between you and the starting point decreases, just like on the graph when Fido is getting closer to home. So, on the graph, the negative slope actually means Fido is moving back towards his home, not that something bad is happening.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh okay, I think I get it now - so the line going down means the distance number is getting smaller, which means Fido is actually moving closer to home, not that he's sleeping or stuck. But wait, if he's moving, shouldn't the line be going up? I'm still a bit confused about why moving towards home makes the line go down instead of up.

score.justification_pass1: The teacher provides correct information through analogies but never directly addresses the student's core misconception (confusing rest with movement), and by Turn 4 the student still fundamentally misunderstands that movement can correspond to a downward slope, showing no real progress.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently grounds the abstract concept of negative slope in concrete, relatable scenarios (watching a movie character's journey, playing a game walking back to a starting point) that connect to everyday experiences the student can visualize.
